scenario.prompt_to_agent:
After an overnight maintenance window, pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports
pings to pc2 (200.1.1.2) are 100% lost, and pc2 reports the same
toward pc1. Yet monitoring shows the router1<->router2 eBGP
session Established with prefixes exchanged, and pc1 can still
ping BOTH of router2's addresses (193.10.11.2 and 200.1.1.1).
Identify what is dropping the traffic.

injection.action: add an iptables FORWARD rule dropping all transit ICMP

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router2 iptables FORWARD chain
Mechanism: a DROP rule for protocol icmp sits in router2's FORWARD
  chain, so any ICMP packet router2 must FORWARD (pc1<->pc2 transit
  in either direction) is discarded at the firewall layer. Traffic
  addressed TO router2 itself traverses INPUT, not FORWARD, which
  is why pc1 can still ping 193.10.11.2 and 200.1.1.1. The BGP
  session is TCP, not ICMP, so it stays Established and all
  prefixes remain exchanged -- routing is completely healthy; the
  drop is purely at the packet-filter layer.
Localization: router2
Root cause: extraneous iptables FORWARD DROP rule for ICMP on
  router2
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -p icmp -j DROP` on router2
scenario.fix_spec:
Remove the DROP rule on router2 -- `iptables -D FORWARD -p icmp -j DROP`.
Transit pings between pc1 and pc2 succeed again immediately; no routing or
BGP change is needed.

agent.diagnosis_text:
Affected component: router2’s packet filter (nftables/iptables) in the FORWARD path. Mechanism: ICMP packets that are being routed through router2 match a blanket “drop ICMP” rule in the FORWARD chain, so host-to-host pings never traverse the router. Direct pings to router2’s own IPs still work because those hit the INPUT path, not FORWARD, and BGP remains Established since it is TCP on local sockets.

Localization: On router2, the nftables filter table, chain FORWARD, contains “meta l4proto icmp … drop.” Evidence: “nft -a list chain ip filter FORWARD” shows “meta l4proto icmp counter … drop # handle 2,” and the counter increments when we attempt pc1→pc2 pings (e.g., packets 11 bytes 924). The legacy view also shows “iptables -S FORWARD … -A FORWARD -p icmp -j DROP.” IP forwarding is enabled (cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward = 1), so the loss is due to filtering, not routing.

Root cause: During the maintenance window, an ICMP drop rule was introduced/left in the FORWARD chain on router2, unintentionally blocking transit ICMP between subnets.

Corrective fix: Remove or disable the ICMP drop rule on router2’s FORWARD chain and, if needed, replace it with a more specific policy. Example: nft delete rule ip filter FORWARD handle 2 (or iptables -D FORWARD -p icmp -j DROP, if managed via iptables-nft). Ensure configuration persistence matches your firewall management method to prevent reintroduction on reboot. After removal, pc1↔pc2 ICMP should succeed.
